title: OSHA Recordkeeping (29 CFR Part 1904)
learningObjectives: Determine whether a work-related injury or illness is recordable
Complete OSHA 300 Log and 301 Incident Report correctly
Calculate total recordable incidence rate (TRIR) and DART rate
Apply Gulf incident reporting and KPI standards used by major operators

content.text: OSHA injury and illness recordkeeping (29 CFR Part 1904) serves three purposes: identifying workplace hazards through trend analysis, tracking the effectiveness of safety programmes, and providing the data that drives OSHA inspection targeting. For HSE professionals, mastering recordkeeping is foundational — incorrect records lead to misleading KPIs and regulatory citations.

Recordkeeping is required for employers with 11 or more employees in industries not on the partially exempt list. Exempt industries include retail, finance, insurance, and real estate (low-hazard industries). ALL employers must report to OSHA: fatalities within 8 hours; inpatient hospitalisation, amputation, or eye loss within 24 hours.

rows: OSHA 300
Log of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses
Running log for the calendar year — every recordable case entered within 7 days
OSHA 301
Injury and Illness Incident Report
Detailed report for each recorded case — how, where, what happened; retain for 5 years
OSHA 300A
Summary of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses
Annual summary posted February 1 – April 30 each year; signed by senior management

content.text: Is the Case Recordable? The Decision Tree
A case is recordable if it is work-related, involves a new case (not a continuation of a pre-existing condition), and meets at least one of the general recording criteria.

items: Days away from work (any lost workdays)
Medical treatment beyond first aid (prescription medication, sutures, physical therapy)
Diagnosis by a healthcare professional as a significant injury or illness (e.g., cancer, chronic irreversible disease, fractured or cracked bone, punctured eardrum)

content.text: Treatment of a minor injury or illness by a layperson or healthcare professional, not requiring ongoing medical treatment. Includes: bandages, antiseptic application, non-prescription medication at non-prescription strength, eye irrigation, removing a splinter, massage. First aid cases are NOT recordable.

A case is work-related if an event or exposure in the work environment either caused or contributed to the injury or illness, or significantly aggravated a pre-existing condition. The work environment includes any location where work activities take place.

rows: Worker trips on wet floor and fractures wrist
YES — work environment, new injury
Worker strains back moving boxes at home after work
NO — not in the work environment
Worker's pre-existing knee pain is aggravated by repetitive kneeling task at work
YES — work activity significantly aggravated the pre-existing condition
Worker has a heart attack at the workplace — no work cause
NO — personal medical event not caused or contributed to by work
Worker cuts finger — washed, bandaged, no further treatment
NO — first aid only

content.text: OSHA rates are calculated per 200,000 hours worked (equivalent to 100 full-time workers for one year at 2,000 hours each). This normalises data to allow comparison across different workforce sizes.

rows: TRIR (Total Recordable Incidence Rate)
(Number of recordable cases x 200,000) / Hours worked
All recordable injuries and illnesses per 200,000 hours
DART Rate (Days Away/Restricted/Transfer)
(DART cases x 200,000) / Hours worked
Only cases involving lost time, restricted duty, or job transfer
LTIR (Lost Time Injury Rate)
(Lost time cases x 200,000) / Hours worked
Only cases with days away from work
Severity Rate
(Days lost x 200,000) / Hours worked
Measures severity, not just frequency
FIFR (Fatal Injury Frequency Rate)
(Fatalities x 1,000,000) / Hours worked
Fatalities per million hours — used in Gulf and international reporting

content.text: A manufacturing plant with 250 employees works 500,000 total hours in a year. They record 8 cases: 3 involving lost workdays, 2 restricted duty, 1 job transfer, 2 medical treatment only. TRIR = (8 x 200,000) / 500,000 = 3.2. DART rate = (3+2+1) x 200,000 / 500,000 = 2.4. The company benchmarks against the BLS industry average to assess performance.

OSHA requires electronic submission of the 300A summary for establishments with 250 or more employees, and establishments with 20–249 employees in high-hazard industries. Submission is through OSHA's Injury Tracking Application (ITA). This public data transparency creates accountability — OSHA publishes establishment-level data.

Gulf Context: Gulf operators use both OSHA-style rates and additional international KPIs. Total Recordable Case Frequency Rate (TRCFR) = TRIR in Gulf terminology. Fatal Injury Frequency Rate (FIFR) = fatalities per million hours — Aramco and ADNOC report FIFR in annual sustainability reports. Near-miss reporting is strongly emphasised in Gulf systems: QatarEnergy targets a near-miss-to-incident ratio of at least 300:1, reflecting a strong near-miss culture. Saudi Arabia's MHRSD (Ministry of Human Resources) requires quarterly injury reporting for all registered businesses. First-aid cases are NOT reported externally but are tracked internally. The International Association of Oil & Gas Producers (IOGP) Report 2019 safety statistics provide the Gulf industry benchmark — HSE professionals should be familiar with the IOGP metrics.
